front_blocks.md: Define **mass**.

back_blocks.md: **Mass** is a measure of the amount of matter in an object; it is the property that resists change in motion.

cards.front_md: Define **mass**.
cards.back_md: **Mass** is a measure of the amount of matter in an object; it is the property that resists change in motion.

front_blocks.md: Define **weight**.

back_blocks.md: **Weight** is the effect of a gravitational field on a mass; it is a force, measured in newtons (N).

cards.front_md: Define **weight**.
cards.back_md: **Weight** is the effect of a gravitational field on a mass; it is a force, measured in newtons (N).

front_blocks.md: State the equation for weight, including the unit of each quantity.

back_blocks.md: $W = m g$

- *W* = weight in newtons (N)
- *m* = mass in kilograms (kg)
- *g* = acceleration of free fall in metres per second squared (m s<sup>-2</sup>)

front_blocks.md: An object in free fall is falling **..........** under the influence of gravitational attraction.

back_blocks.md: An object in free fall is falling **solely** under the influence of gravitational attraction.

cards.front_md: An object in free fall is falling **..........** under the influence of gravitational attraction.
cards.back_md: An object in free fall is falling **solely** under the influence of gravitational attraction.

front_blocks.md: In the absence of air resistance, how does the acceleration of falling objects near Earth's surface compare for different masses?

back_blocks.md: All bodies fall with the **same acceleration**, regardless of their mass.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An object's mass decreases when it is taken to the Moon.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
An object's **mass** remains the same wherever it is; only its **weight** changes, because the gravitational field strength differs.

front_blocks.md: Define **resultant force**.

back_blocks.md: The **resultant force** is the vector sum of all the forces acting on a body.

cards.front_md: Define **resultant force**.
cards.back_md: The **resultant force** is the vector sum of all the forces acting on a body.

front_blocks.md: State the equation relating force, mass and acceleration, including units.

back_blocks.md: $F = m a$

- *F* = force in newtons (N)
- *m* = mass in kilograms (kg)
- *a* = acceleration in metres per second squared (m s<sup>-2</sup>)

front_blocks.md: The acceleration of an object is always in the **..........** direction as the resultant force acting on it.

back_blocks.md: The acceleration of an object is always in the **same** direction as the resultant force acting on it.

cards.front_md: The acceleration of an object is always in the **..........** direction as the resultant force acting on it.
cards.back_md: The acceleration of an object is always in the **same** direction as the resultant force acting on it.

front_blocks.md: A resultant force acts on an object in the opposite direction to its motion. What effect does this have on the object?

back_blocks.md: The object **decelerates** (slows down), since the resultant force opposes the direction of motion.

cards.front_md: A resultant force acts on an object in the opposite direction to its motion. What effect does this have on the object?
cards.back_md: The object **decelerates** (slows down), since the resultant force opposes the direction of motion.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The resultant force acting at an angle to an object's motion can be found by simple arithmetic addition of the forces.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Since force is a **vector**, a resultant force acting at an angle must be found using **vector addition**, not simple addition.

front_blocks.md: Define **linear momentum**.

back_blocks.md: **Linear momentum** is the product of an object's mass and velocity: $p = m v$, measured in kilogram metres per second (kg m s<sup>-1</sup>).

cards.front_md: Define **linear momentum**.
cards.back_md: **Linear momentum** is the product of an object's mass and velocity: $p = m v$, measured in kilogram metres per second (kg m s<sup>-1</sup>).

front_blocks.md: Why is momentum described as a vector quantity?

back_blocks.md: Because it has both **magnitude** and **direction**; it can have a positive or negative value depending on the direction of motion.

cards.front_md: Why is momentum described as a vector quantity?
cards.back_md: Because it has both **magnitude** and **direction**; it can have a positive or negative value depending on the direction of motion.

front_blocks.md: A ball travelling to the right has positive momentum, so an identical ball travelling to the left has **..........** momentum.

back_blocks.md: A ball travelling to the right has positive momentum, so an identical ball travelling to the left has **negative** momentum.

cards.front_md: A ball travelling to the right has positive momentum, so an identical ball travelling to the left has **..........** momentum.
cards.back_md: A ball travelling to the right has positive momentum, so an identical ball travelling to the left has **negative** momentum.

front_blocks.md: A tennis ball and a brick have equal momentum, despite the brick having a far greater mass. Explain how this is possible.

back_blocks.md: Momentum depends on both **mass** and **velocity**; the tennis ball has a much lower mass but a much greater velocity than the brick, so their products (*mv*) are equal.

cards.front_md: A tennis ball and a brick have equal momentum, despite the brick having a far greater mass. Explain how this is possible.
cards.back_md: Momentum depends on both **mass** and **velocity**; the tennis ball has a much lower mass but a much greater velocity than the brick, so their products (*mv*) are equal.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An object with a greater mass will always have greater momentum than a lighter object.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Momentum depends on the product of mass and velocity, not mass alone; a lighter, faster object can have the same or greater momentum than a heavier, slower one.

cards.front_md:

cards.back_md:
**False.**

front_blocks.md: Define **force** in terms of momentum.

back_blocks.md: **Force** is the rate of change of momentum: $F = \frac{Δp}{Δt}$

cards.back_md: **Force** is the rate of change of momentum: $F = \frac{Δp}{Δt}$

front_blocks.md: State the equation for change in momentum.

back_blocks.md: $Δ p = p_{f} - p_{i}$ where *p*<sub>f</sub> is the final momentum and *p*<sub>i</sub> is the initial momentum.

front_blocks.md: For a given change in momentum, increasing the **..........** taken for an impact decreases the force exerted.

back_blocks.md: For a given change in momentum, increasing the **time** taken for an impact decreases the force exerted.

cards.front_md: For a given change in momentum, increasing the **..........** taken for an impact decreases the force exerted.
cards.back_md: For a given change in momentum, increasing the **time** taken for an impact decreases the force exerted.

front_blocks.md: A car exerts a force of 300 N on a wall during a collision. State the magnitude and direction of the force the wall exerts on the car.

back_blocks.md: The wall exerts a force of **300 N** on the car, in the **opposite direction** to the force the car exerts on the wall (Newton's third law).

cards.front_md: A car exerts a force of 300 N on a wall during a collision. State the magnitude and direction of the force the wall exerts on the car.
cards.back_md: The wall exerts a force of **300 N** on the car, in the **opposite direction** to the force the car exerts on the wall (Newton's third law).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Increasing the time over which a collision occurs, for the same change in momentum, increases the force experienced.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Increasing the time **decreases** the force experienced, since $F = \frac{Δp}{Δt}$

front_blocks.md: Define **Newton's first law** of motion.

back_blocks.md: A body will remain at rest or move with constant velocity unless acted on by a **resultant force**.

cards.front_md: Define **Newton's first law** of motion.
cards.back_md: A body will remain at rest or move with constant velocity unless acted on by a **resultant force**.

front_blocks.md: Define **Newton's second law** of motion.

back_blocks.md: A resultant force acting on a body causes a change in the body's motion in the **direction of the force**: $F = m a$

cards.front_md: Define **Newton's second law** of motion.
cards.back_md: A resultant force acting on a body causes a change in the body's motion in the **direction of the force**: $F = m a$

front_blocks.md: Define **Newton's third law** of motion.

back_blocks.md: Whenever two bodies interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal** in magnitude and **opposite** in direction.

cards.front_md: Define **Newton's third law** of motion.
cards.back_md: Whenever two bodies interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal** in magnitude and **opposite** in direction.

front_blocks.md: State the four conditions required for a pair of forces to be a Newton's third law force pair.

back_blocks.md:
- Same **type** of force
- Same **magnitude**
- **Opposite** in direction
- Acting on **different objects**

front_blocks.md: If the forces acting on an object are balanced, the object is said to be in **..........**.

back_blocks.md: If the forces acting on an object are balanced, the object is said to be in **equilibrium**.

cards.front_md: If the forces acting on an object are balanced, the object is said to be in **..........**.
cards.back_md: If the forces acting on an object are balanced, the object is said to be in **equilibrium**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Two equal and opposite forces acting on the same object form a Newton's third law pair.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

A Newton's third law pair must act on **different objects**; two equal and opposite forces on the same object (e.g. weight and normal contact force) are an example of **equilibrium** (Newton's first law), not the third law.
